los.text: Describe the main respiratory causes of a patient with wheeze and describe the most common and appropriate investigations to aid diagnosis of respiratory disorders
los.html:
WheezePolyphonic (diffuse airway narrowing) or monophonic (single fixed obstruction, e.g. tumour or foreign body). Stridor is inspiratory and upper airway.
CausesAsthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, LRTI/viral bronchiolitis, heart failure ("cardiac asthma"), anaphylaxis, tumour/foreign body, vocal cord dysfunction.
FeatureAsthmaCOPD
OnsetOften young, atopic>35, smoker/exposure
VariabilityMarked, diurnal, triggersPersistent, progressive
Night symptomsCommonUncommon
SputumUncommonChronic productive cough
ReversibilitySignificantLimited
  • Investigations: spirometry (FEV1/FVC <0.7 = obstruction) with bronchodilator reversibility
    • PEFR diary (variability)
    • FeNO (eosinophilic inflammation)
    • CXR (hyperinflation, exclude cancer/HF)
    • FBC (eosinophils, polycythaemia)
    • ABG if hypoxic
    • α1-antitrypsin if young/never smoked
    • BNP/echo if HF suspected
    • CT if bronchiectasis or nodules.

los.text: Describe the structure and functions of the upper and lower respiratory tract
sessions: Clin 2: Introduction to the respiratory system
los.html:
Upper tract(nose → larynx)Warms, humidifies and filters air (turbinates, mucus, cilia); olfaction; phonation (larynx); protects airway (epiglottis, cough reflex).
Lower tract
  • Trachea (C-shaped cartilage rings)
  • → main bronchi (right is wider, shorter, more vertical, so aspirated objects go right)
  • → lobar
  • → segmental
  • → bronchioles (no cartilage)
  • → terminal bronchioles (end of conducting zone, ≈150 mL anatomical dead space)
  • → respiratory bronchioles
  • → alveolar ducts
  • → alveoli (respiratory zone).
Epithelium
  • Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells
  • → cuboidal (Club cells) in bronchioles
  • → type I pneumocytes (thin, gas exchange, ~95% of surface) and type II (surfactant, progenitors).
  • Alveolar macrophages clear debris.
Mucociliary escalator clears particles; impaired by smoking and in CF/PCD.
Surfactant (DPPC) lowers surface tension → prevents alveolar collapse (Laplace) and increases compliance.
FunctionsGas exchange, acid–base (CO₂), ACE conversion of angiotensin I, filter for emboli, reservoir of blood.

los.text: Describe the signs, symptoms, pathophysiology and common morphological changes in patients with chronic airway obstruction, with particular reference to COPD (chronic bronchitis and emphysema)
los.html:
COPDPersistent airflow limitation (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7) that is progressive, usually from smoking (also biomass fuel, occupational dusts, α1-antitrypsin deficiency).
SymptomsExertional breathlessness, chronic cough, sputum, frequent winter "bronchitis", wheeze.
Signs
  • Hyperinflated barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing, accessory muscles, ↓ cricosternal distance, hyper-resonance, quiet breath sounds, wheeze
  • Cor pulmonale (raised JVP, peripheral oedema)
  • CO₂ retention flap
  • Tar staining.
Chronic bronchitis(clinical definition)
  • Productive cough ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years.
  • Morphology: mucous gland hypertrophy (Reid index >0.4), goblet cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia, small-airway fibrosis and narrowing.
Emphysema(pathological definition)
  • Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles with wall destruction.
  • Centriacinar (upper lobes, smoking) vs panacinar (lower lobes, α1-antitrypsin deficiency).
  • Bullae.
Pathophysiology
  • Smoke
  • → neutrophils/macrophages
  • → protease (elastase) > antiprotease imbalance + oxidative stress
  • → loss of elastic recoil
  • → airways collapse on expiration
  • → air trapping, hyperinflation, V/Q mismatch
  • → hypoxaemia ± hypercapnia
  • → pulmonary vasoconstriction
  • → pulmonary hypertension
  • → cor pulmonale.
Old labels: "pink puffer" (emphysema) vs "blue bloater" (bronchitis).

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat COPD and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
Non-drug firstSmoking cessation (the only thing that slows FEV1 decline, with LTOT for survival), pulmonary rehabilitation (MRC ≥3), flu/pneumococcal/COVID vaccines, inhaler technique.
Step 1SABA (salbutamol) or SAMA (ipratropium) as needed.
Step 2 (NICE NG115)No asthmatic features → LABA + LAMA (e.g. salmeterol/formoterol + tiotropium). Asthmatic/steroid-responsive features (eosinophilia, variability, atopy) → LABA + ICS.
Step 3Triple therapy LABA + LAMA + ICS if still exacerbating or symptomatic.
DrugMechanismKey side effects
β2 agonists (SABA/LABA)β2 → Gs → ↑cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxationTremor, tachycardia, ↓K⁺
Antimuscarinics (SAMA/LAMA)Block M3 → ↓ bronchoconstriction and mucusDry mouth, urinary retention, glaucoma
ICSAnti-inflammatory gene effectsOral candidiasis, dysphonia, ↑ pneumonia risk in COPD
TheophyllinePDE inhibitionNarrow therapeutic index; arrhythmias, seizures; CYP450 interactions
OthersRoflumilast (PDE4i), prophylactic azithromycin (non-smokers with frequent exacerbations; check ECG/QTc and LFTs), mucolytics (carbocisteine).
Exacerbation
  • Increase bronchodilators, prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days, antibiotics if purulent sputum (amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin).
  • Controlled O₂ target 88–92%
  • NIV if pH <7.35 with ↑PaCO₂ despite treatment.
LTOTPaO₂ <7.3 kPa (or <8 kPa with polycythaemia, peripheral oedema or pulmonary hypertension) on two readings, in non-smokers; ≥15 h/day.

los.text: Explain how carbon dioxide is transported in blood and describe the effects of hypo- and hyper-ventilation on PCO2 levels and their relationship with pH
los.html:
CO₂ carriage~70% as bicarbonate, ~20–23% as carbamino compounds (bound to Hb), ~7–10% dissolved.
  • In RBCs: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (via carbonic anhydrase) ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.
  • HCO₃⁻ leaves in exchange for Cl⁻ (chloride shift, band 3).
  • H⁺ is buffered by deoxy-Hb.
Haldane effectDeoxygenated Hb carries more CO₂ (tissues load CO₂; lungs unload it).
PaCO₂ is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation: PaCO₂ ∝ VCO₂ / VA.
Hypoventilation↑PaCO₂ → ↑H⁺ → ↓pH (respiratory acidosis).
Hyperventilation↓PaCO₂ → ↑pH (respiratory alkalosis) → ↓ ionised Ca²⁺ → tingling, carpopedal spasm.
Henderson–HasselbalchpH = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × PaCO₂ in mmHg)), i.e. pH depends on the HCO₃⁻ : CO₂ ratio.

los.text: Explain the causes of ‘metabolic’ and ‘respiratory’ acidosis and alkalosis and the body’s compensatory mechanisms
los.html:
DisorderPrimary changeCausesCompensation
Respiratory acidosis↑PaCO₂COPD, opioids, neuromuscular weakness, chest wall disease, obesity hypoventilationKidneys ↑ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption and H⁺ excretion (days)
Respiratory alkalosis↓PaCO₂Anxiety, PE, pain, early asthma, high altitude, salicylate (early)Kidneys ↓ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption
Metabolic acidosis↓HCO₃⁻DKA, lactic acidosis, AKI, toxins; diarrhoea, RTAHyperventilation (Kussmaul), within minutes
Metabolic alkalosis↑HCO₃⁻Vomiting, diuretics, hypokalaemia, Conn'sHypoventilation (limited by hypoxia)
Anion gap
  • (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), normal ≈ 10–18 (or 8–12 without K⁺).
  • High gap (added acid, "MUDPILES"): methanol, uraemia, DKA, paraldehyde, iron/isoniazid, lactate, ethylene glycol, salicylates.
  • Normal gap (hyperchloraemic): loss of HCO₃⁻ (diarrhoea, ileostomy), renal tubular acidosis, Addison's, acetazolamide, excess saline.
BuffersBicarbonate (main ECF), Hb, proteins, phosphate; then lungs (minutes) and kidneys (days).
Compensation never overcorrects. A "normal" pH with abnormal CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ suggests a mixed disorder.

los.text: Describe the mechanisms of oxygen transport in the blood and summarise the factors that affect this
sessions: BMS 2: Oxygen transport in the blood
los.html:
98.5% bound to haemoglobin, ~1.5% dissolved (Henry's law: 0.003 mL O₂/dL/mmHg).
Each Hb binds 4 O₂ cooperatively → sigmoid dissociation curve. 1 g Hb carries 1.34 mL O₂.
O₂ content(1.34 × Hb × SaO₂) + (0.003 × PaO₂). O₂ delivery = cardiac output × content.
Right shift(↓ affinity, unloads O₂ in tissues)↑CO₂, ↑H⁺ (Bohr effect), ↑temperature, ↑2,3-BPG (altitude, anaemia), exercise.
Left shift(↑ affinity)Opposite changes, fetal Hb (HbF), carbon monoxide, methaemoglobin.
CO poisoningCO binds Hb ~240× more avidly and left-shifts the curve. Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal; use co-oximetry (COHb).
AnaemiaNormal PaO₂ and SaO₂ but low O₂ content.
MyoglobinSingle chain, hyperbolic curve, stores O₂ in muscle.

los.text: Describe the mechanisms of ventilation (inhalation and exhalation)
los.html:
Inspiration (active)
  • Diaphragm contracts and descends (phrenic nerve C3–5) + external intercostals lift ribs (pump-handle and bucket-handle movements)
  • → ↑ thoracic volume
  • → intrapleural pressure falls (≈ −5 to −8 cmH₂O)
  • → alveolar pressure below atmospheric
  • → air flows in (Boyle's law).
Expiration (quiet, passive)Elastic recoil of lungs and chest wall.
Forced expirationInternal intercostals + abdominal muscles. Forced inspiration: accessory muscles (SCM, scalenes, pectorals).
ComplianceΔV/ΔP. ↓ in fibrosis, oedema, ARDS, surfactant deficiency. ↑ in emphysema (loss of elastic tissue).
PleuraThe fluid film couples the lung to the chest wall; negative intrapleural pressure keeps lungs expanded (lost in pneumothorax).

los.text: Explain the regulation of airflow in and out of the lungs and define respiratory cycle, respiratory rate, tidal volume, alveolar ventilation, and minute volume
sessions: BMS 3: Airflow regulation and volume definitions
los.html:
• Airway resistance (Poiseuille: R ∝ 1/r⁴) is greatest in medium-sized bronchi.
  • Small airways contribute little because there are so many in parallel.
BronchoconstrictionParasympathetic (vagus, M3, ACh), histamine, leukotrienes, cold air, irritants.
Bronchodilationβ2 stimulation (circulating adrenaline; little direct sympathetic innervation), NO, ↑ lung volume (radial traction).
Dynamic compressionin forced expiration, airways collapse at the equal pressure point; worse with loss of elastic recoil (emphysema).
Respiratory cycleOne inspiration + one expiration.
Respiratory rate12–20 breaths/min in adults.
Tidal volume (VT)~500 mL (≈7 mL/kg) per quiet breath.
Minute ventilationVT × RR ≈ 6 L/min.
Alveolar ventilation
  • (VT − dead space) × RR ≈ (500 − 150) × 12 ≈ 4.2 L/min.
  • Rapid shallow breathing wastes more as dead space.
  • Other volumes: IRV ~3 L, ERV ~1.2 L, RV ~1.2 L
  • FRC = ERV + RV
  • VC = IRV + VT + ERV
  • TLC ≈ 6 L.
  • RV and FRC (and TLC) can't be measured by spirometry.

los.text: Explain the concept of public health (the public health approach)
sessions: MHS 1: Communicable diseases 1: The public health approach
los.html:
Public health(Acheson)"the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through the organised efforts of society."
Focus on populations rather than individuals; addresses the wider determinants of health.
Three domainsHealth protection (communicable disease, environmental hazards), health improvement (lifestyle, inequalities, education), healthcare quality (service planning, efficiency, audit).
Public health approachDefine the problem (surveillance, epidemiology) → identify risk and protective factors → develop and test interventions → implement at scale and evaluate.
Levels of preventionPrimary (stop disease: vaccines, smoking cessation), secondary (detect early: screening), tertiary (reduce impact: rehab).
Rose's prevention paradox
  • a measure that brings large benefit to the population offers little to each individual.
  • Population strategies shift the whole risk curve.
For communicable disease: surveillance, notification, outbreak control, contact tracing, immunisation. UK bodies: UKHSA (England), Public Health Wales.
